questions.stem: What does 「雨がふらないうちに帰りましょう。」 mean?
options: Let's go home because it isn't raining.
Let's go home before it starts raining.
Let's go home after the rain stops.
Let's go home even though it is raining.
questions.explanation: FF + 「うちに」 means while a state lasts, so 「ふらないうちに」 is 'while it is not yet raining', that is, before the rain starts. Going home after the rain stops would need 「やんでから」.

questions.stem: What does 「たくさん勉強したのに、テストはむずかしかったです。」 mean?
options: If I study a lot, the test will be hard.
I studied a lot, so the test was easy.
Even though I studied a lot, the test was hard.
Because I studied a lot, the test was hard.
questions.explanation: 「のに」 links two ideas where the second is not what the first would lead you to expect: 'even though'. Reading it as a reason confuses 「のに」 with 「ので」.

questions.stem: Which word completes 「この店は安い___、いつもすいています。」 ('Even though this shop is cheap, it is always empty')?
questions.explanation: The gloss calls for 'even though', which is 「のに」: a cheap shop would be expected to be busy. 「ので」 and 「から」 give a reason, and 「し」 lists reasons, so all three make cheapness the cause of the shop being empty.

questions.stem: What does 「雪になるみたいですね。」 mean?
options: It looks as if it will turn to snow.
It snowed a lot, didn't it?
I want it to turn to snow.
questions.explanation: FF + 「みたい」 expresses how something appears: the speaker judges from what they can see that snow is likely. It is a guess, not a certainty, so 'definitely' overstates it.

questions.stem: What does 「りんごみたいなくだもの」 mean?
options: an apple and some other fruit
a fruit that I like more than apples
questions.explanation: NOUN + 「みたいな」 + noun describes something by likeness: 'a fruit like an apple'. 「みたいな」 behaves like a な adjective before a noun, and it says nothing about preference.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「日本に___前に、ひらがなをおぼえました。」 ('Before going to Japan, I learnt hiragana')?
questions.explanation: FF + 「前に」 always takes the non-past plain form, even when the whole sentence is in the past, because the going had not yet happened. 「行った前に」 is a common error.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「しゅくだいを___後で、友だちに会いました。」 ('After doing my homework, I met a friend')?
questions.explanation: 「〜た後で」 takes the plain past form, since the homework was finished first. 「して」 would need 「から」 after it (「してから」) to mean after.

questions.stem: What does 「テレビを見るより本を読むほうが楽しいです。」 mean?
options: Reading books is more fun than watching TV.
Watching TV is more fun than reading books.
Reading books and watching TV are equally fun.
I read books while watching TV.
questions.explanation: FF + 「より」 marks what is being compared against, and 「〜ほうが」 marks the one that is more so. Here reading takes 「ほうが」, so reading is the more enjoyable one.

questions.stem: In 「すずきさんの書いた手紙を読みました。」, what does 「の」 do?
options: It shows that Suzuki owns the letter now
It joins Suzuki and the letter as a list
It marks Suzuki as the one who wrote the letter, like が
It shows the letter is about Suzuki
questions.explanation: Inside a clause that describes a noun, 「の」 can replace 「が」 as the subject marker, so 「すずきさんの書いた手紙」 means the letter Suzuki wrote. Reading it as plain possession misses that 「書いた」 is the verb of a describing clause.

questions.stem: What is the difference between 「すしを食べることがあります。」 and 「すしを食べたことがあります。」?
options: The first: I sometimes eat sushi. The second: I have eaten sushi before.
The first: I have eaten sushi before. The second: I sometimes eat sushi.
The first: I can eat sushi. The second: I have decided to eat sushi.
The first: I want to eat sushi. The second: I used to eat sushi.
questions.explanation: Non-past FF + 「ことがあります」 says something happens on occasion, while past 「〜た」 + 「ことがあります」 relates an experience. The tense of the verb before 「こと」 is what changes the meaning.

questions.stem: Which sentence shows that a move was decided by circumstances, not by the speaker?
options: 「来年、おおさかに住むことになりました。」
「来年、おおさかに住むことにしました。」
「来年、おおさかに住むことができます。」
「来年、おおさかに住んだことがあります。」
questions.explanation: 「ことになる」 presents an outcome that was settled for you, for example by a parent's job, while 「ことにする」 is a decision the speaker made. 「住んだことがあります」 cannot go with 「来年」, since it describes past experience.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「三月から日本語をならい___ました。」 ('I began learning Japanese in March')?
questions.explanation: ます base + 「はじめる」 means to begin doing, so 「ならい」 + 「はじめ」 + 「ました」 gives 「ならいはじめました」. 「はじまる」 is intransitive (something begins) and does not attach to a verb's ます base this way.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「はやく本を___なさい。」 ('Read the book quickly')?
questions.explanation: 「なさい」 attaches to the ます base: 「読みます」 → 「読み」 → 「読みなさい」. The plain and て forms do not take 「なさい」.

questions.stem: Who would most naturally say 「はやくねなさい。」, and to whom?
options: A junior worker to a manager
A parent to a young child
A shop assistant to a customer
questions.explanation: ます base + 「なさい」 is a firm command used from above, typically by parents or teachers to children. Said to a teacher, customer or manager it would be rude.

questions.stem: What does 「このじしょはとても使いやすいです。」 mean?
options: This dictionary is very easy to use.
This dictionary is very hard to use.
I really want to use this dictionary.
questions.explanation: ます base + 「やすい」 says something is easy to do, here easy to use. The opposite pattern, ます base + 「にくい」, means hard to do.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「朝ご飯を___学校に行きました。」 ('I went to school without eating breakfast')?
questions.explanation: ない base + 「ないで」 links two actions as 'without doing', which is what the gloss needs. 「食べなくて」 gives a cause, as in 'I didn't eat, so...', and 「食べなかって」 is not a form at all.

questions.stem: What does 「テレビを見ないで勉強しなさい。」 mean?
options: You don't have to study or watch TV.
questions.explanation: 「見ないで」 links the two actions, 'without watching', and 「勉強しなさい」 is a command to study. It is not a request to stop studying.

questions.stem: How do you ask a friend not to open the window?
options: 「まどをあけなくてもいいです。」
「まどをあけないでもいいです。」
「まどをあけないでください。」
questions.explanation: ない base + 「ないでください」 requests that someone not do something. 「あけなくてもいい です」 says they don't have to open it, which leaves the choice to them rather than asking.

questions.stem: Which form completes 「ひま___、テレビは見ません。」 ('Even if I'm free, I don't watch TV')?
questions.explanation: With nouns and な adjectives, 'even if' is 「でも」: 「ひまでも」. 「くても」 is for い adjectives, as in 「高くても」, which is the slip students make.

questions.stem: What extra meaning does 「しゅくだいをわすれてしまいました。」 carry?
options: Attempt: the speaker tried to forget it
Regret: the speaker is sorry it happened
Intention: the speaker forgot on purpose
Habit: the speaker always forgets it
questions.explanation: Besides finishing something, 「〜てしまう」 shows that the speaker regrets an action or that it happened against their wishes. Nothing in the form suggests a habit or a deliberate choice.

questions.stem: What does 「はやく行けば、道はこんでいません。」 mean?
options: Go early, because the roads are crowded.
If you go early, the roads won't be crowded.
Even if you go early, the roads are crowded.
When I went early, the roads weren't crowded.
questions.explanation: The ば form 「行けば」 expresses a condition: if you go early. The result clause says the roads will not be crowded, so it is not the 'even if' of 「ても」.

questions.stem: What is the ば form of 「行く」?
questions.explanation: For an う verb, the final sound moves to the え row and takes 「ば」: 「く」 → 「け」, giving 「行けば」. 「行くば」 adds 「ば」 to the dictionary form, which is the usual slip.

questions.stem: What is the potential form of 「話す」?
questions.explanation: For an う verb the potential uses the え row + 「る」: 「す」 → 「せ」, giving 「話せる」. 「話させる」 is the causative, 'make someone talk', a different form.

questions.stem: What is the potential form of 「来る」 in standard written Japanese?
questions.explanation: 「来る」 is irregular: its potential is 「こられる」, as in 「明日来られますか」. 「くれる」 is the verb of giving to me, and 「こらえる」 is an unrelated verb meaning to endure.

questions.stem: What does 「さしみが食べられます。」 mean?
questions.explanation: For a る verb, ない base + 「られる」 gives the potential, 'can eat', and 「が」 marks what can be eaten. The NSW list gives it for receptive use alongside the える form.

questions.stem: What is the plain volitional form of 「来る」, as in 「日本へ___と思います。」?
questions.explanation: 「来る」 is irregular and its volitional is 「こよう」, so 「日本へこようと思います」 expresses an intention to come to Japan. 「くろう」 wrongly treats it as an う verb.

questions.stem: Which particle marks the giver in 「友だち___本をかしてもらいました。」 ('I had a friend lend me a book')?
questions.explanation: With 「〜てもらう」 the receiver is the subject and the giver is marked with 「に」. 「が」 would suit 「友だちがかしてくれました」, which looks at the same favour from the giver's side.

questions.stem: Which verb completes 「私は妹にケーキを作って___。」 ('I made a cake for my younger sister')?
questions.explanation: 「〜てあげる」 is used when the speaker does a favour for someone else. 「くれる」 and 「くださる」 are for favours done for the speaker, so they cannot have 「私は」 as the giver.

questions.stem: Which verb completes 「田中先生に駅まで車でおくって___。」 ('I had Tanaka-sensei kindly drive me to the station')?
questions.explanation: 「に」 marks the teacher as the giver, which fits only a receiving verb, and for a superior that is 「いただく」. 「くださる」 is equally polite but needs 「先生が」, with the teacher as subject.

questions.stem: What does 「お金が少しもありません。」 mean?
options: I need a little more money.
I don't have any money at all.
I have only a little money.
I have a little money as well.
questions.explanation: A quantity word + 「も」 + a negative means not even a little, that is, none at all. 'Only a little' would be 「少ししかありません」.

questions.stem: In a shop, what does 「の」 stand for in 「赤いのをください。」?
options: The item already being talked about
The colour red as a noun
questions.explanation: The nominaliser 「の」 replaces a noun both speakers already have in mind, so this means 'the red one, please'. It is not the possessive 「の」.

questions.stem: What does the sentence-final 「わ」 add in 「きれいだわ。」?
options: Uncertainty about whether it is true
Mild emphasis, used mainly in feminine speech
A firm command to the listener
questions.explanation: The NSW list gives 「わ」 as mild emphasis, traditionally feminine. Asking for agreement is the job of 「ね」.
